title: U.S. House · Iowa's 1st District
area: Southeast Iowa, including Davenport, Burlington, Ottumwa, and Fort Madison

context.text: Incumbent Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R) advanced from the June 2, 2026 Republican primary and is running for a third term representing this district (she previously represented the old 2nd District, 2021-2023). Christina Bohannan (D), a former state representative and University of Iowa law professor, is her Democratic challenger for a third consecutive cycle. Cook Political Report rated the district R+4.

candidates.name: Mariannette Miller-Meeks
candidates.ballotNote: Advanced from the June 2 Republican primary
candidates.currentRole: U.S. Representative, Iowa's 1st District (since 2023); previously represented the 2nd District (2021-2023)

summary.text: Mariannette Miller-Meeks is the Republican incumbent for Iowa's 1st District, seeking a fourth term. A physician and U.S. Army veteran, she ran unsuccessfully for Congress three times before winning in 2020 by six votes, and previously led the Iowa Department of Public Health and served in the Iowa Senate. She is running on her record in Congress, including her work on health care and veterans' issues.

background.text: Born in Herlong, California (September 6, 1955, according to Wikipedia). According to her official biography, she was the fourth of eight children and left home at 16 to attend community college.

Earned a bachelor's degree in nursing from Texas Christian University (1976), a master's degree from the University of Southern California (1980), and a medical degree from the University of Texas Health Science Center (1986).

Served in the U.S. Army for 24 years as a private, nurse, and doctor, according to her official biography. Wikipedia lists active duty from 1976 to 1982 and Army Reserve service from 1983 until she retired in 2000.

Practiced as an ophthalmologist, running a private practice in Ottumwa, Iowa, until 2008, and was the first woman in two decades on the University of Iowa ophthalmology faculty, according to Wikipedia.
Was the Republican nominee for Iowa's 2nd Congressional District in 2008, 2010, and 2014, losing to Democrat Dave Loebsack each time.
Served as director of the Iowa Department of Public Health from 2010 to 2014, appointed by Gov. Terry Branstad.
Was elected to the Iowa Senate (District 41) in 2018 and served until January 2021, when she resigned to join the U.S. House.

Won the 2020 race for the 2nd District by six votes after a recount over Democrat Rita Hart, who later withdrew a challenge to the result. She won re-election in the renumbered 1st District in 2022 (53.4 percent) and in 2024 (by 799 votes after a recount), both over Christina Bohannan.

Serves on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, including its Health subcommittee, and on the Veterans' Affairs Committee, where she is chair of the Health Subcommittee. According to her official biography, she has two grown children.
Won the June 2026 Republican primary over David Pautsch.

priorities.text: Promote U.S. energy production and independence, including expanded oil, gas, and biofuels production and streamlined permitting.
Strengthen border security and immigration enforcement.

positions.summary: Miller-Meeks's issues page criticizes restrictions on fossil fuel production and describes cosponsoring the Lower Energy Costs Act to expand oil, gas, and mineral production and streamline permitting.
Official press release says the Laken Riley Act, which she championed, requires detention of immigrants without legal status who are charged with theft or with killing or seriously injuring a person.
positions.quote: This critical bipartisan legislation ensures that illegal aliens charged or convicted of theft, like the individual responsible for Laken Riley’s tragic death, will be detained to prevent further harm.

positions.summary: In a May 2026 letter to Senate leaders, urged a Senate vote on the House-passed SAVE Act, which requires documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote.
positions.quote: It is imperative that the Senate immediately schedule the House-passed Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act and advance the bill to President Trump's desk for his signature into Law.

record.text: Cosponsored H.R. 1, the Lower Energy Costs Act, aimed at ending restrictions on energy production and streamlining permitting; it passed the House with bipartisan support.
Introduced the Critical Infrastructure Manufacturing Feasibility Act, which passed the House and directs a federal study on domestic manufacturing of critical-infrastructure goods.
Introduced the Refrigerator Freedom Act, which passed the House and limits the Department of Energy's authority to implement certain appliance efficiency regulations.
Led efforts to allow year-round sale of E15 fuel in Iowa and nationally.

Serves on the House Committee on House Administration (Elections subcommittee), the Committee on Energy and Commerce (Health, Energy, and Environment subcommittees), and chairs the Health Subcommittee of the House Committee on Veterans' Affairs, 2025-2026.

candidates.name: Christina Bohannan
candidates.currentRole: Former member, Iowa House of Representatives

summary.text: Christina Bohannan is the Democratic nominee, an engineer-turned-law professor at the University of Iowa who served one term in the Iowa House (2021-2023). She lost to Miller-Meeks in 2022 and by 799 votes in 2024 and is challenging her for a third time. Her campaign centers on lowering costs and reducing the influence of special-interest money in Congress.

background.text: Grew up in a small town in a family she describes as non-political; her father was a construction worker and her mother worked part-time at a daycare. She says she was the first in her family to go to college.
Earned a degree in environmental engineering and a law degree, both from the University of Florida; she says she graduated first in her law school class.

Worked as an environmental engineer with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection, specializing in water quality, then clerked for a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit, according to Wikipedia.
Has taught at the University of Iowa College of Law since about 2000, and served as president of its faculty senate, according to Wikipedia.

Won the 2020 Democratic primary for Iowa House District 85, defeating incumbent Vicki Lensing, and served in the Iowa House from 2021 to 2023, including on the Natural Resources and Veterans Affairs committees.
Was the 2022 Democratic nominee for Iowa's 1st District, losing to Miller-Meeks 53.4 to 46.6 percent, and lost the 2024 rematch 50.0 to 49.8 percent.
Announced a third run in June 2025 and won the June 2026 Democratic primary. According to Wikipedia, she is married, has a daughter, and lives in Iowa City.

priorities.text: Lower costs for Iowans by ending broad tariffs, capping insulin costs at $35 per month, and letting Medicare negotiate lower prescription drug prices.
Prohibit hedge funds and private investors from buying up family homes and land, and build and rehabilitate more housing.
Reduce the influence of special-interest and corporate campaign money in Congress.

positions.summary: Bohannan's platform calls for Congress to end broad tariffs, which she says have raised costs for Iowa families and farmers.
positions.quote: Exercising Congress's power to end the disastrous tariffs that are one of the biggest tax increases in American history and have left Iowans to pay thousands per year in higher costs

positions.summary: Bohannan's platform calls for prohibiting hedge funds and private investors from buying up family homes and land.
Bohannan's platform calls for letting Medicare negotiate lower prescription drug prices and capping insulin costs at $35 per month for everyone.
Bohannan's platform calls for expanding Iowa's clean energy economy and cracking down on utility monopolies to lower energy bills.
Voted no on HF 756 (removing the permit requirement to carry a handgun), which passed the Iowa House 60-37 on 2021-03-17.
Voted no on HF 2317 (replacing Iowa's graduated income tax with a 3.9% flat tax), which passed the Iowa House 61-37 on 2022-02-16.

record.text: Voted no on HF 756 (removing the permit requirement to carry a handgun in Iowa), which passed the Iowa House 60-37 on 2021-03-17.
Voted no on SF 413 (an elections bill shortening the absentee-voting window and tightening voter-list maintenance), which passed the Iowa House 57-37 on 2021-02-24.
Voted no on HF 2317 (replacing Iowa's graduated income tax with a 3.9% flat tax), which passed the Iowa House 61-37 on 2022-02-16.

candidates.name: Michael Bridgford

summary.text: Michael Bridgford is an independent candidate and a Bettendorf-based financial advisor. He grew up on a family farm near the Quad Cities and holds an MBA from Northwestern University. His campaign centers on lowering costs and government-reform measures such as term limits and a ban on congressional stock trading.

background.text: Says he grew up on a seventh-generation family farm near the Quad Cities, which is still in the family, and attended public schools with a graduating class of 88.
Earned an MBA from Northwestern University.
Says he has worked in financial services, technology, and logistics, previously co-owned a small logistics business, and now works with his father in their financial advisory business.
Announced his campaign in April 2026 as an independent challenging Republican incumbent Miller-Meeks; Iowa Public Radio described him as the only independent in the race at that time.
Says his campaign collected more than 3,500 petition signatures across all 20 counties in 40 days. He says he lives in Bettendorf with his wife and two daughters.

priorities.text: Says he would focus on popular, nonpartisan issues such as legislation on term limits and a ban on congressional stock trading.
Names affordability, agriculture and health care as top priorities, and says he would push for price transparency and pharmacy benefit manager reform.

Campaign website lists priorities including term limits, a congressional stock trading ban and campaign finance reform; fixing Social Security; and healthcare price transparency and revitalization of rural clinics.

candidates.researchNotes: Bridgford has not completed Ballotpedia's Candidate Connection survey. His campaign website (bridgfordforiowa.com/issues) shows one-line headings with no body text, so only the headings are cited as priorities. Statements come from Iowa Public Radio (Apr. 16, 2026), Independent Voter News (Aug. 12, 2026) and Iowa Capital Dispatch (Aug. 15, 2026). Nothing found on abortion, guns, tariffs or other listed issues.

statements.quote: I just don't see any plausibility to those being put in place in the next two years.
statements.context: Interview with Independent Voter News (Aug. 12, 2026), asked about Medicare for All, a public option and enhanced ACA subsidies; he said he would pursue price transparency instead

statements.quote: we have community members that have been here a long time, contributing, being rounded up. The answer is in the middle.
statements.context: Interview with Iowa Public Radio, April 16, 2026

statements.quote: I do think we are at a point that if we are going to escalate, that's where Congress needs to be involved

researchNotes: Miller-Meeks's tariff position is only documented through her opponent's campaign materials (a candidate source about the other candidate), not through Miller-Meeks's own statements; treat with appropriate caution. Bohannan's own record as a state legislator was not itemized bill-by-bill within the research budget. Bridgford's biography relies on his Ballotpedia profile and Candidate Connection survey plus Iowa Public Radio; no campaign site was loaded. Miller-Meeks's early-career details (Army Reserve dates, ophthalmology practice, 2008-2014 runs) come from Wikipedia and are not on her official page.
